top_level_objectives: Understand how the mutual repulsion of electron domains determines the three-dimensional shape of molecules.
Identify and construct the five fundamental electron-domain geometries (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral).
Differentiate between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Explain how lone pair electrons compress bond angles and alter idealized molecular geometries, using real-world examples like water and ammonia.
Successfully predict the 3D molecular geometry of a molecule given its 2D Lewis structure.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 1: The Core Concept of Repulsion
scenes.brief_purpose: To introduce the fundamental concept of VSEPR theory: that electron domains repel one another to maximize distance and minimize energy.
key_visuals: A central atom floating in space with an interactive 'add bond' holographic button.
Glowing energy fields representing electron domains that physically push away from each other.
Dynamic angle labels that update in real-time as domains move.
student_actions: Add two electron domains to a central atom and observe them snap to a 180-degree Linear geometry.
Add a third domain and watch the bonds shift into a flat 120-degree Trigonal Planar arrangement.
Physically walk around the 3D hologram to verify that the arrangement remains entirely flat (2D).

scenes.brief_purpose: To demonstrate how adding a fourth electron domain forces the molecule to break out of a 2D plane and into a 3D tetrahedral shape.
key_visuals: A 3D model of Methane (CH4) forming from a generic central atom setup.
A wireframe tetrahedron encapsulating the molecule to highlight the geometric shape.
A 109.5-degree angle marker spanning multiple H-C-H bonds.
student_actions: Add a fourth domain to a trigonal planar structure and observe the transformation into a 3D tetrahedral shape.
Grab and rotate the methane molecule in AR space to see that all four positions are structurally identical.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 3: The Impact of Lone Pairs
scenes.brief_purpose: To illustrate the difference between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry, and how lone pairs affect bond angles.
key_visuals: Side-by-side holographic models of Methane (CH4), Ammonia (NH3), and Water (H2O).
Large, diffuse, semi-transparent clouds representing lone pair electrons.
A digital protractor tool for measuring bond angles.
student_actions: Toggle the lone pair clouds on and off to see how the visible 'molecular geometry' differs from the 'electron-domain geometry' (Trigonal Pyramidal and Bent).
Use the digital protractor to measure the bond angles of methane (109.5°), ammonia (107°), and water (104.5°).
Observe an animation showing the larger lone pair clouds physically compressing the adjacent bonding pairs.

scenes.brief_purpose: To explore expanded octets with five domains, introducing the concepts of axial and equatorial positions.
key_visuals: A model of Phosphorus pentafluoride (PF5) with axial positions colored red and equatorial positions colored blue.
Holographic text overlays showing 90-degree and 120-degree bond angles.
student_actions: Identify and select the axial vs. equatorial positions using a laser pointer tool.
Convert one bonding pair into a lone pair and observe it selectively replacing an equatorial bond to minimize 90-degree repulsions, forming a 'Seesaw' shape.
Continue replacing bonds with lone pairs to discover the T-shaped and Linear molecular geometries.

scenes.brief_purpose: To explore the symmetrical octahedral electron-domain geometry and its common molecular shape derivatives.
key_visuals: Models of Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) and Xenon tetrafluoride (XeF4).
Animated indicators showing all six positions are initially equivalent, unlike the 5-domain model.
student_actions: Add six bonding domains to form a perfect octahedral SF6 molecule with 90-degree angles.
Replace one bond with a lone pair to form a Square Pyramidal shape.
Replace a second bond with a lone pair, observing that it naturally positions itself 180 degrees away from the first to form a flat Square Planar shape (XeF4).

scenes.brief_purpose: To test the student's ability to apply VSEPR rules to predict 3D geometry from 2D representations.
key_visuals: A virtual whiteboard displaying the 2D Lewis structures of various randomized molecules (e.g., CO2, SO2, BrF5).
An empty central atom workspace with an inventory of bonds and lone pair clouds.
A 'Check Answer' terminal that provides visual and auditory feedback.
student_actions: Analyze the given 2D Lewis structure and determine the correct number of bonding and non-bonding electron domains.
Construct the 3D molecule by dragging the correct number of bonds and lone pairs onto the central atom.
Select the correct names for both the electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry from a floating menu to complete the lab.
